lessons.title: Ohm law and references
lessons.formula: U = R I; P = U I = I²R
lessons.text: Choose a current arrow and measure the resistor voltage drop along it. A negative result means the actual direction is opposite. Use ohm, volt and ampere consistently.
lessons.trap: A negative current is not an error. A resistor still dissipates non-negative power.

lessons.title: Equivalent resistance
lessons.text: Series elements share the same current with no branch at their joining node. Parallel elements share both electrical nodes. Redraw wires as nodes before reducing a network.
lessons.trap: Visual proximity does not prove series or parallel. Changing the measurement terminals can change the answer.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff current law
lessons.formula: Sum of signed currents at a node = 0
lessons.text: Pick entering currents positive or leaving currents positive and stay consistent. In a connected network, one node equation is dependent on the others.
lessons.trap: Writing both A and B equations for a two-node network does not create two independent equations.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff voltage law
lessons.formula: Sum of signed voltages around a closed loop = 0
lessons.text: Choose a loop direction. A voltage rise and a voltage drop have opposite signs. Write Ohm law for each resistor and enough independent node/loop constraints.
lessons.trap: The ideal current source voltage is generally unknown. Do not pretend it has zero voltage.

lessons.title: Superposition
lessons.formula: Total response = signed sum of single-source responses
lessons.text: In a linear circuit, leave one independent source active at a time. Replace other ideal voltage sources by shorts and current sources by opens. Keep resistors and dependent sources.
lessons.trap: Add voltage or current contributions, then calculate power. Do not add the separately calculated powers.

lessons.title: Capacitors and inductors
lessons.formula: Q = C V; iC = C dV/dt; vL = L dI/dt
lessons.text: Capacitors store electric-field energy; inductors store magnetic-field energy. In settled ideal DC, a capacitor is open and an inductor is short.
lessons.trap: The steady-state simplification does not describe the switching transient.

lessons.title: Sinusoidal AC
lessons.text: Resistor voltage and current are in phase. Capacitor current leads its voltage by 90 degrees; inductor current lags its voltage by 90 degrees. For a sine wave, RMS = peak/sqrt(2).
lessons.trap: Reactance magnitude is positive, while capacitor impedance has a negative imaginary part. The sine-wave RMS conversion is not universal.

lessons.title: Thevenin and Norton
lessons.formula: VTh = Voc; IN = Isc; RN = RTh; VTh = IN RTh
lessons.text: A linear two-terminal network has a voltage-source/series-resistance or current-source/parallel-resistance equivalent. These reproduce terminal behavior; they do not reproduce every internal branch.
lessons.trap: Disconnect the load when finding the equivalent. Keep dependent sources active; use a test source when needed. This section is theory-focused for the reported exam.

steps: Identify nodes joined by ideal wires before combining components.

fields.label: Equivalent resistance

exercises.title: Loaded voltage divider
exercises.prompt: Find the output voltage Uab, current in R1 (S to A), and power dissipated by R1. V1 = 24 V.

fields.label: Uab
fields.explanation: The load R3 is in parallel with R2.

fields.label: R1 current, S to A
fields.explanation: I1 = (V1 - Uab) / R1.

fields.label: R1 power
fields.explanation: P1 = I1² R1. Power dissipated by a resistor is non-negative.

steps: Rload = R2 || R3 = 120 ohm.
Uab = V1 * Rload / (R1 + Rload) = 12 V.
exercises.hint: A loaded divider uses the parallel combination of the lower resistor and load.

exercises.title: Resistor power budget
exercises.prompt: Find the output voltage Uab, current in R1 (S to A), and power dissipated by R1. V1 = 12 V.

fields.label: Uab
fields.explanation: The load R3 is in parallel with R2.

fields.label: R1 current, S to A
fields.explanation: I1 = (V1 - Uab) / R1.

fields.label: R1 power
fields.explanation: P1 = I1² R1. Power dissipated by a resistor is non-negative.

steps: Rload = R2 || R3 = 120 ohm.
Uab = V1 * Rload / (R1 + Rload) = 8 V.
exercises.hint: A loaded divider uses the parallel combination of the lower resistor and load.

exercises.title: A negative current is meaningful
exercises.prompt: Calculate current in R1 using the reference B to A, and voltage V(B) - V(A).

fields.label: R1 current, B to A
fields.explanation: The actual current runs from A to B, opposite to the requested reference.

fields.label: V(B) - V(A)
fields.explanation: The requested voltage reference is opposite to the drop along the actual current.

steps: Total resistance is 900 ohm, so the physical current is 9/900 = 0.01 A from A to B.
Reversing a reference changes the sign: I = -0.01 A and U = -3 V.
exercises.hint: Read the requested direction before calculating.

exercises.title: Sharing a current source
exercises.prompt: Find currents through R1 and R2 from the upper rail to the lower rail, and the voltage between the rails.

fields.label: R1 current
fields.explanation: Current divides inversely with resistance.

steps: Both branches have 4 V across them; 0.02 + 0.01 = 0.03 A.
exercises.hint: The smaller resistance carries the larger current.

exercises.title: Write the complete equation set
exercises.prompt: Define I1 from S through R1 and R2 toward A; I2 from A through R3 and R5 to B; I3 from C through R4 to D. U1…U5 are resistor drops along those currents. Vs is the voltage of V1. Write five Ohm laws, KCL at A and B, and the two stated KVL loops. Use * for multiplication.

fields.label: Ohm law for R1
fields.explanation: U1 is measured along I1; use the passive sign convention.

fields.label: Ohm law for R2
fields.explanation: U2 is measured along I1; use the passive sign convention.

fields.label: Ohm law for R3
fields.explanation: U3 is measured along I2; use the passive sign convention.

fields.label: Ohm law for R4
fields.explanation: U4 is measured along I3; use the passive sign convention.

fields.label: Ohm law for R5
fields.explanation: U5 is measured along I2; use the passive sign convention.

fields.label: KCL at A
fields.explanation: I1 enters A; I2 and I3 leave.

fields.label: KCL at B
fields.explanation: This is the negative of the A equation, not an additional independent constraint.

fields.label: KVL: source and middle branch
fields.explanation: The voltage rise of the source equals the drops along the left/middle loop.

fields.label: KVL: middle and right branches
fields.explanation: Both paths join A and B, so their total voltage drops agree.

steps: Each resistor contributes U = R*I using its branch current.
At A: I1 = I2 + I3. At B the same conservation law has the opposite sign.
Left loop: Vs = U1 + U2 + U3 + U5. Right loop: U3 + U5 = U4.
There are two independent meshes; writing KCL for both essential nodes does not give two independent equations.
exercises.hint: Do not give R1 and R2 different branch currents: no current leaves their joining node.

exercises.title: One node, three branches
exercises.prompt: I1 runs S to A, I2 runs A to B and I3 runs C to D. U1, U2 and U3 are drops along those currents. Vs is V1. Write the requested relations.

fields.label: KCL at A
fields.explanation: One current enters and two leave.

fields.label: KVL through R1 and R2
fields.explanation: Follow the source rise, then both resistor drops.

fields.label: Equal parallel voltages
fields.explanation: R2 and R3 connect the same two electrical nodes.

steps: KCL: I1 - I2 - I3 = 0.
KVL: Vs - U1 - U2 = 0.
The lower branches are parallel, so U2 = U3.
exercises.hint: You may rearrange or multiply a complete equation by a non-zero constant.

exercises.title: Build a nodal equation
exercises.prompt: Let U be the voltage at A relative to B; Vs is V1. Write KCL at A entirely in U, Vs and resistor values. Then express the R2 current I2 from A to B.

fields.label: Nodal KCL
fields.explanation: Sum currents leaving A: (U - Vs)/R1, U/R2 and U/R3.

fields.label: R2 current
fields.explanation: The bottom of R2 is the reference node.

steps: Translate each outgoing current into a voltage difference divided by resistance.
Once U is known, I2 = U/240.
exercises.hint: Choose all branch currents leaving the node, even if one result becomes negative.

exercises.title: A current-source constraint
exercises.prompt: Js denotes J1. I1 and I2 run down R1 and R2. U is the upper-rail voltage relative to the lower rail. Write KCL, both Ohm laws, and a voltage-only node equation.

fields.label: KCL at the upper rail
fields.explanation: The current source injects Js into the upper rail.

fields.label: Ohm law for R1
fields.explanation: R1 shares the rail voltage U.

fields.label: Ohm law for R2
fields.explanation: R2 shares the same rail voltage.

fields.label: Voltage-only KCL
fields.explanation: Replace the two resistor currents using Ohm law.

steps: Js = I1 + I2.
exercises.hint: An ideal current source fixes current; its voltage is determined by the network.

exercises.title: Voltage and current cooperate
exercises.prompt: Use superposition to find current in R2, referenced from A to B, then its total power. Use the source selector to inspect each reduced circuit. All sources are independent and ideal.

fields.label: R2 current: V1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep V1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R2 current: J1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep J1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R2 total current
fields.explanation: Add the signed contributions; do not add their magnitudes.

fields.label: R2 total power
fields.explanation: Compute power from the total current: P = I_total² R. Individual source powers cannot be superposed.

steps: V1 alone: open J1. R1 and R2 are in series, so the downward R2 current is V1/(R1+R2).
J1 alone: short V1. R1 and R2 are parallel, so the R2 contribution has magnitude J1*R1/(R1+R2). Its sign is positive for injection into the upper node and negative for extraction.
With V1 alone, V(A) - V(B) = 8 V, so I = 0.04 A.
With J1 alone, V(A) - V(B) = 2 V, so I = 0.01 A.
exercises.hint: For V1 alone use a divider; for J1 alone, R1 and R2 are parallel.

exercises.title: An opposing current source
exercises.prompt: Use superposition to find current in R2, referenced from A to B, then its total power. Use the source selector to inspect each reduced circuit. All sources are independent and ideal.

fields.label: R2 current: V1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep V1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R2 current: J1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep J1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R2 total current
fields.explanation: Add the signed contributions; do not add their magnitudes.

fields.label: R2 total power
fields.explanation: Compute power from the total current: P = I_total² R. Individual source powers cannot be superposed.

steps: V1 alone: open J1. R1 and R2 are in series, so the downward R2 current is V1/(R1+R2).
J1 alone: short V1. R1 and R2 are parallel, so the R2 contribution has magnitude J1*R1/(R1+R2). Its sign is positive for injection into the upper node and negative for extraction.
With V1 alone, V(A) - V(B) = 8 V, so I = 0.04 A.
With J1 alone, V(A) - V(B) = -6 V, so I = -0.03 A.
exercises.hint: The current-source contribution is negative in the requested downward reference.

exercises.title: When the total current reverses
exercises.prompt: Use superposition to find current in R2, referenced from A to B, then its total power. Use the source selector to inspect each reduced circuit. All sources are independent and ideal.

fields.label: R2 current: V1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep V1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R2 current: J1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep J1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R2 total current
fields.explanation: Add the signed contributions; do not add their magnitudes.

fields.label: R2 total power
fields.explanation: Compute power from the total current: P = I_total² R. Individual source powers cannot be superposed.

steps: V1 alone: open J1. R1 and R2 are in series, so the downward R2 current is V1/(R1+R2).
J1 alone: short V1. R1 and R2 are parallel, so the R2 contribution has magnitude J1*R1/(R1+R2). Its sign is positive for injection into the upper node and negative for extraction.
With V1 alone, V(A) - V(B) = 6 V, so I = 0.01 A.
With J1 alone, V(A) - V(B) = -12 V, so I = -0.02 A.
exercises.hint: A negative answer is valid. Keep the sign through the final sum.

exercises.title: Two voltage sources, one load
exercises.prompt: Use superposition to find current in R2, referenced from A to B, then its total power. Use the source selector to inspect each reduced circuit. All sources are independent and ideal.

fields.label: R2 current: V1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep V1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R2 current: V2 alone
fields.explanation: Keep V2 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R2 total current
fields.explanation: Add the signed contributions; do not add their magnitudes.

fields.label: R2 total power
fields.explanation: Compute power from the total current: P = I_total² R. Individual source powers cannot be superposed.

steps: At A, KCL is (Ua-V1)/R1 + Ua/R2 + (Ua-V2)/R3 = 0.
Let G = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. Then Ua due to V1 is (V1/R1)/G; Ua due to V2 is (V2/R3)/G. Divide each by R2 for its load-current contribution.
With V1 alone, V(A) - V(B) = 9.81818 V, so I = 0.0409091 A.
With V2 alone, V(A) - V(B) = 1.09091 V, so I = 0.00454545 A.
exercises.hint: When one source is shorted, its series resistor remains in the circuit.

exercises.title: The zero-contribution surprise
exercises.prompt: Use superposition to find current in R3, referenced from C to D, then its total power. Use the source selector to inspect each reduced circuit. All sources are independent and ideal.

fields.label: R3 current: J1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep J1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R3 current: V1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep V1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R3 total current
fields.explanation: Add the signed contributions; do not add their magnitudes.

fields.label: R3 total power
fields.explanation: Compute power from the total current: P = I_total² R. Individual source powers cannot be superposed.

steps: V1 fixes V(A)-V(B). With V1 alone, R2 and R3 form a series load: I_R3 = V1/(R2+R3).
With J1 alone, V1 is a short. Both ends of the R2-R3 series path are at the same potential, so its current is zero. The left source current returns through the short.
With J1 alone, V(C) - V(D) = 0 V, so I = 0 A.
With V1 alone, V(C) - V(D) = 9 V, so I = 0.03 A.
exercises.hint: With V1 switched off, A is shorted to B. Can the left current source change the right-hand voltage?

exercises.title: Two current sources meet
exercises.prompt: Use superposition to find current in R1, referenced from A to B, then its total power. Use the source selector to inspect each reduced circuit. All sources are independent and ideal.

fields.label: R1 current: J1 alone
fields.explanation: Keep J1 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R1 current: J2 alone
fields.explanation: Keep J2 active. Replace every other ideal voltage source by a short and every other ideal current source by an open circuit.

fields.label: R1 total current
fields.explanation: Add the signed contributions; do not add their magnitudes.

fields.label: R1 total power
fields.explanation: Compute power from the total current: P = I_total² R. Individual source powers cannot be superposed.

steps: With J1 alone, all its injected current returns through R1: I_R1 = J1.
With J2 alone, it extracts current from the upper rail, so I_R1 = -J2. The combined KCL equation is J1 - J2 - I_R1 = 0.
With J1 alone, V(A) - V(B) = 6 V, so I = 0.04 A.
With J2 alone, V(A) - V(B) = -1.5 V, so I = -0.01 A.
exercises.hint: Switching off a current source opens its branch. The remaining current source drives R1.

exercises.prompt: At 50 Hz, calculate the magnitude of the ideal component reactance. Give a positive magnitude, not complex impedance.
steps: Convert the value to SI units: 1e-05 F.
omega = 2*pi*50 rad/s.

exercises.title: Peak is not RMS
exercises.prompt: A sinusoidal voltage has a peak amplitude of 170 V and drives a 100 ohm resistor. Find RMS voltage and average resistor power.

fields.label: RMS voltage
fields.explanation: For a sine wave, Vrms = Vpeak / sqrt(2).

fields.label: Average power
fields.explanation: Paverage = Vrms²/R, not Vpeak²/R.

exercises.hint: The peak-to-RMS conversion here applies specifically to a sine wave.

exercises.title: Charge and stored energy
exercises.prompt: An ideal 47 microfarad capacitor is charged to 12 V. Calculate its stored charge and energy.

fields.label: Stored charge
fields.explanation: Q = C*V. Convert microfarads to farads.

fields.label: Stored energy
fields.explanation: E = C*V²/2.

exercises.hint: Use SI units throughout.

exercises.title: What does Ohm law state?
exercises.prompt: For an ideal resistor at fixed conditions, which relation holds?

fields.label: Choose one answer
fields.explanation: Voltage drop is proportional to current, with resistance as the proportionality factor.

steps: Voltage drop is proportional to current, with resistance as the proportionality factor.
exercises.hint: Explain the physical law before comparing the choices.

exercises.title: Why does KCL work?
exercises.prompt: The algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero because of:

fields.label: Choose one answer
fields.explanation: Charge does not accumulate at an ideal circuit node; entering and leaving currents balance.

steps: Charge does not accumulate at an ideal circuit node; entering and leaving currents balance.
exercises.hint: Explain the physical law before comparing the choices.

exercises.title: Which loop statement is valid?
exercises.prompt: For a lumped circuit with no unmodelled time-varying magnetic flux, KVL says:

fields.label: Choose one answer
options: The algebraic voltage sum around a closed loop is zero
Every resistor has the same voltage
fields.expected: The algebraic voltage sum around a closed loop is zero
fields.explanation: Use a consistent traversal direction and include source rises and element drops.

steps: Use a consistent traversal direction and include source rises and element drops.
exercises.hint: Explain the physical law before comparing the choices.

exercises.title: Deactivate sources correctly
exercises.prompt: For superposition with independent ideal sources, how are inactive sources replaced?

fields.label: Choose one answer
options: Voltage source: short; current source: open
Voltage source: open; current source: short
fields.expected: Voltage source: short; current source: open
fields.explanation: Setting ideal voltage to zero constrains its terminals to equal potential. Setting ideal current to zero blocks its branch.

steps: Setting ideal voltage to zero constrains its terminals to equal potential. Setting ideal current to zero blocks its branch.
exercises.hint: Explain the physical law before comparing the choices.

exercises.title: Can powers be superposed?
exercises.prompt: Two source contributions to resistor current are I_a and I_b. Total resistor power is:

fields.label: Choose one answer
fields.explanation: Voltage and current are linear responses. Power is quadratic, so use the signed total current before squaring.

steps: Voltage and current are linear responses. Power is quadratic, so use the signed total current before squaring.

exercises.prompt: In an ideal capacitor, the current:

fields.label: Choose one answer
options: Is always in phase with voltage
fields.explanation: i = C*dV/dt. For a sine-wave voltage, differentiation gives a quarter-cycle lead.

steps: i = C*dV/dt. For a sine-wave voltage, differentiation gives a quarter-cycle lead.

exercises.title: Inductor in sinusoidal steady state
exercises.prompt: In an ideal inductor, the voltage:

fields.label: Choose one answer
options: Is always in phase with current
fields.explanation: v = L*dI/dt; the voltage leads sinusoidal current by a quarter cycle.

exercises.title: Ideal storage elements after settling
exercises.prompt: In DC steady state, an ideal capacitor and ideal inductor behave as:

fields.label: Choose one answer
fields.explanation: Constant capacitor voltage gives zero capacitor current. Constant inductor current gives zero inductor voltage. This is a steady-state statement, not the switching transient.

steps: Constant capacitor voltage gives zero capacitor current. Constant inductor current gives zero inductor voltage. This is a steady-state statement, not the switching transient.

exercises.title: Recognize a Thevenin equivalent
exercises.prompt: A linear two-terminal network can be represented by:

fields.label: Choose one answer
options: An ideal voltage source in series with an equivalent resistance
An ideal voltage source in parallel with a resistance
A resistor that must equal the load
fields.expected: An ideal voltage source in series with an equivalent resistance
fields.explanation: Thevenin voltage is the open-circuit terminal voltage. Equivalent resistance is seen looking into the unloaded network; independent sources are deactivated for the passive resistance method.

steps: Thevenin voltage is the open-circuit terminal voltage. Equivalent resistance is seen looking into the unloaded network; independent sources are deactivated for the passive resistance method.
exercises.hint: Explain the physical law before comparing the choices.

exercises.title: Connect Norton and Thevenin
exercises.prompt: For matching terminal references and a finite positive equivalent resistance:

fields.label: Choose one answer
options: I_N always equals the load current
R_N = R_Th and V_Th = I_N * R_Th
fields.expected: R_N = R_Th and V_Th = I_N * R_Th
fields.explanation: Norton uses an ideal current source in parallel with the equivalent resistance. I_N is the short-circuit terminal current under the chosen reference convention.

steps: Norton uses an ideal current source in parallel with the equivalent resistance. I_N is the short-circuit terminal current under the chosen reference convention.
exercises.hint: Explain the physical law before comparing the choices.

exercises.prompt: When finding an equivalent resistance in a network containing dependent sources:

fields.label: Choose one answer
options: Keep dependent sources active and use a test source if necessary
fields.expected: Keep dependent sources active and use a test source if necessary
fields.explanation: Only independent sources are deactivated. A dependent source still obeys its controlling relation.

steps: Only independent sources are deactivated. A dependent source still obeys its controlling relation.

exercises.title: Connect an ideal meter
exercises.prompt: How should voltage and current be measured?

fields.label: Choose one answer
options: Voltmeter in series; ammeter in parallel
Voltmeter in parallel; ammeter in series
fields.expected: Voltmeter in parallel; ammeter in series
fields.explanation: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance. Real instruments approximate these limits.

steps: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance. Real instruments approximate these limits.
